opus-5.5.text:
I don't think so, at least not in the strong sense the question implies. It's a really common concern, and I get why people raise it. If you're collecting data from human hands doing tasks, it seems natural to assume the robot has to look like a human to use it. But I think that conflates two different things: the *kinematics* of the demonstration and the *intent* or *structure* of the task.

What human data gives you, more than anything, is a huge amount of information about what matters in a task. Where you look, what you attend to, which objects are relevant, the order of subgoals, what contact needs to happen, roughly where things need to end up. A lot of that is pretty embodiment-agnostic. If a person is wiping a table, the fact that the sponge needs to sweep across the surface with some pressure doesn't really depend on whether it's held by five fingers or a parallel-jaw gripper or a suction cup.

So in our work we try to think about representations that sit at the right level of abstraction. Things like object-centric trajectories, keypoint motion, or how the scene should change, rather than literally retargeting joint angles from a human hand onto a robot. Once you're at that level, the robot's own controller and its own learned low-level policy can figure out how to realize that with whatever body it has. You can have a robot with more degrees of freedom, fewer, wheels instead of legs, a gripper instead of a hand, and still benefit from the human prior.

There's a related point. Human data is most valuable at scale and for diversity, the long tail of environments and tasks you'd never cover with robot teleoperation alone. You typically pair it with a smaller amount of robot-specific data that grounds those priors in the robot's actual body. The human data tells you "what" and a lot of "why"; the robot data fills in "how, for this embodiment." That co-training setup is where we've seen the most benefit.

Now, I'll be honest that there is some bias. If you lean too heavily on directly imitating human motion, you'll inherit human habits that might be suboptimal for a robot. A robot might be able to do something more efficiently by rotating its wrist 360 degrees or by using two arms in ways people wouldn't. So I don't think human data should be the ceiling. It's a really good starting point, a prior, and then things like reinforcement learning or self-improvement can let the robot discover strategies that exploit its own body.

So my short answer: human data shapes what robots understand about tasks, but it doesn't have to dictate their bodies. And honestly, I'm excited about non-humanoid designs that still learn a ton from watching people.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot with more degrees of freedom than the human demonstrator can still use human task data, and that its own controller can realize the demonstrated task with its body.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think the honest answer is: only if you let it.

There's a distinction I always try to draw between learning from human data and learning to imitate humans literally. If you take a mocap dataset and retarget it joint-for-joint onto a humanoid, then yes, you've basically baked in the human kinematic chain. Your robot inherits our shoulders, our wrists, our two hands with five fingers each, and it inherits our limitations too. If it has a third arm or a wrist that can spin 360 degrees, that data just doesn't know what to do with it.

But I don't think that's the right way to think about what human data is for. To me, the value of human data is mostly at the level of intent and strategy, not at the level of joint trajectories. When I watch someone open a cabinet, the useful thing to extract is "grasp the handle, pull along this arc, keep the other hand clear" — the task structure, the contact sequence, the affordances. That's largely embodiment-agnostic. How you execute it with your particular actuators is a separate problem, and that's where things like reinforcement learning, trajectory optimization, or just a learned low-level controller for your specific morphology come in.

So the way we've approached it in my group is to think of human data as a prior on what to do, and then let the robot's own experience figure out how to do it. Sometimes that means an intermediate representation — object-centric keypoints, end-effector trajectories, a plan in some abstract action space — and then a per-robot policy that grounds it. The nice thing is that if you do it that way, a robot with extra degrees of freedom can actually exploit them. It might find a solution a human never would, because the human never had that option.

I'd also add that there's a practical reason human-ish morphology has been winning lately, and it's not just the data. Our world is built for human bodies. Door handles, stairs, tools — they're all shaped by our hands and our reach. So even a robot that could be anything has a reason to be somewhat human-shaped. But I'd say that's a consequence of the environment, not of the learning method.

Where I do get worried is the case where people conflate the two — where the only way we know how to get good data is teleoperation with a human-matched device, and so the hardware gets designed to match the teleop rig, and now the whole pipeline is locked into one body. That's a real risk. But it's a choice we're making in how we collect and represent data, not something fundamental about learning from humans.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot with extra degrees of freedom can use human data and find a different solution, but it does not clearly state that the robot can imitate a system with fewer mechanical degrees of freedom.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think so. I think it depends on what you’re trying to learn from the human data. If you’re trying to copy every joint movement directly, then yes, you’re assuming a pretty similar body. But human demonstrations can tell you a lot more than that: what the goal is, which objects matter, how to break a task into steps, and what happens when you interact with the world.

Imagine watching someone open a drawer. The useful thing to learn isn’t necessarily the exact trajectory of their elbow. It’s that you need to grasp the handle and pull in a particular direction. A robot with a very different arm could accomplish that using its own motion.

The challenge is connecting that human data to the robot’s capabilities. You still need some way for the robot to learn how its own body works, through robot data, simulation, or interaction. So I see human data as a source of knowledge, rather than a constraint that says the robot has to be shaped like us.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot with a very different arm can use its own motion to accomplish a demonstrated task, but it does not state that the robot has more mechanical degrees of freedom than the system it imitates.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think so. Learning from human data doesn’t mean copying human joint motions directly. A lot of what we want to learn is at the level of intent: what are you trying to accomplish, what objects matter, and how do you interact with them? Those things can transfer across different bodies.

The robot still needs to learn how to realize that behavior with its own hardware. If it has an extra arm or a different kind of gripper, human demonstrations won’t directly tell it how to use those capabilities. But they can provide a starting point, and then robot experience can fill in the gap. So human data is useful guidance, rather than a constraint that the robot has to have the same degrees of freedom as us.

r001.rationale: The response says human demonstrations can guide a robot with an extra arm and that learning transfers across different bodies, so the robot can learn behavior from a system with fewer degrees of freedom.
